stem: static (int min, int max) MinMax(int[] a) returns:
options: ONE tuple value with named members .min and .max
explanation: Tuples bundle values with no type declaration - the modern replacement for paired out parameters (1.9).

stem: (int low, int high, _) = Analyse(data); The _ is:
options: A DISCARD - that component is deliberately ignored
explanation: Deconstruction splits the tuple into locals; _ marks the parts you do not want without inventing a name.

explanation: Value semantics come free - which also makes tuples usable as composite dictionary keys.

stem: A tuple crossing a PUBLIC API boundary usually wants to become:
options: A record - fixed, documented member names instead of per-usage ones
explanation: Tuples suit private helpers and quick pairs; the same shape renamed slightly at every call site is how confusion breeds. Records fix the names (2.9).

stem: (p1, p2) switch { ("rock", "scissors") => ..., (var x, var y) when x == y => "draw", ... } matches on:
options: The COMBINATION of both values - rock-paper-scissors as a table of cases
explanation: Positional patterns over a tuple turn paired logic into a readable truth table - compare with the nested-if version.

stem: order switch { { Country: "UK", Amount: > 50 } => "free", ... } is matching on:
options: The VALUES of its properties - no casts, no temporaries
explanation: Property patterns read like the pricing table a human would write - which is exactly the point.

stem: values switch { [] => "empty", [var only] => ..., [1, ..] => "starts with 1", ... } - the .. means:
options: A SLICE: any number of items here
explanation: List patterns (C# 11) match on shape: emptiness, exact lengths, first/last elements, with .. absorbing the middle.

stem: Circle(var r) when r > 5 => "big" works on a record because records generate:
options: Deconstruct - so positional patterns can take them apart
explanation: The generated Deconstruct (2.9) is what positional matching calls. Records + switch = functional-style modelling with exhaustiveness help.

stem: Prefer a pattern SWITCH over virtual methods when:
options: The logic spans several values/shapes, or the data types cannot be given methods
explanation: Behaviour belonging to the type, types added often -> virtual (2.6). Cross-cutting rules over shapes, cases added often -> patterns. Complementary tools.

explanation: Build a tuple, deconstruct into the opposite slots. You have been using tuple machinery since lesson 5.3.
